extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy (Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and evaluate the competing definitions and arguments about the nature of justice presented in Book I of Plato's Republic (Cephalus, Polemarchus, Thrasymachus, and Socrates' responses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as speaking the truth and paying debts
rubrics_metrics.description: Cephalus' tentative definition: justice consists in telling the truth and repaying one's debts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates raises counterexamples (e.g., returning weapons to a friend who is insane would be harmful), showing the definition is too simple and admits exceptions; the passage suggests such literal formulations require qualification or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as repayment of debts (Simonides' formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simonides is quoted as saying that the repayment of a debt is justice — expressed as giving to each what is 'due' or 'proper' to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes ambiguity in 'debt' and 'due' (a deposit returned to an insane friend is a 'debt' yet returning it may be unjust). Socrates pushes for clarifying what 'due' means (ultimately interpreted as 'what is proper').

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as giving good to friends and harm to enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: Polemarchus (interpreting Simonides) defines justice as the art which gives benefits to friends and harms to enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates examines analogies to arts (physician, pilot, soldier) and shows this definition leads to troublesome implications: it makes justice useful only when items are to be kept (not used), and it implies the just man might be a thief. The dialogue presses for refinement and tests the definition with examples and logical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friend/enemy must be truly good/bad (not merely seeming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction offered: when calling someone a friend or enemy, we should mean those who are truly good (friends) or truly bad (enemies), not merely those who seem so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This move attempts to fix the earlier definition by restricting 'friend' and 'enemy' to moral status; Socrates then interrogates whether even with this restriction justice can consist in harming enemies, leading to further rejection of the injuring-account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice cannot consist in injuring anyone
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates' argument: to injure a person makes them worse in their proper function/virtue; since the good cannot produce bad (an art does not make its subject worse), a just person cannot rightly injure another — thus justice cannot be the practice of harming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates uses analogies (musician can't make people unmusical) and a reductio: if justice made people worse it would be self-contradictory. This is used as a decisive objection to definitions of justice that include harming enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as the interest of the stronger (Thrasymachus' claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrasymachus' bold thesis: justice is nothing other than the interest of the stronger (the ruling power); laws are made by rulers for their own interest and what they command constitutes justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He supports this by pointing to different regimes (tyranny, democracy, aristocracy) making laws in their own interest. Socrates challenges it by noting rulers can err; Thrasymachus replies by redefining 'stronger/ruler' strictly (so a true ruler does not err). The dialogue explores whether equating justice with power/advantage holds under scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as obedience to rulers' commands (laws as justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit in Thrasymachus' account: justice = obedience to the laws/commands issued by those in power (those who rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates points out that if rulers make mistaken laws (contrary to their real interest), then obedience would force subjects to act against the rulers' interest, undermining the thesis; Thrasymachus replies by insisting the ruler, insofar as he is a true ruler, doesn't err — a linguistic/analytical move the dialogue scrutinizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler in the strict sense is unerring (Thrasymachus' technical move)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrasymachus' clarification: when he speaks of the 'stronger' he means the ruler in the strict (true) sense — a ruler, properly speaking, is unerring and always commands what is for his interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a semantic rescue: instead of conceding rulers sometimes err, Thrasymachus narrows 'ruler' to exclude mistaken rule. Socrates then tests consequences by analogy to crafts (true physicians don't intend to make money but to heal), interrogating whether this salvage suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each art aims at the interest/perfection of its subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates' general principle: every art or craft has an 'interest' (telos) which is the perfection or proper good of that art's subject — e.g., medicine aims at the health of bodies; pilot aims at the safe guidance of ship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is employed to question Thrasymachus' account: if ruling is an art, its 'interest' would be the perfection of the governed (or of rulership), not simply the rulers' private advantage; the passage uses examples (medicine, piloting) to clarify the notion of 'interest' as telos rather than private gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice useful for safekeeping (deposits) but not for productive use
rubrics_metrics.description: Polemarchus argues justice is useful when one wants to keep possessions safe (e.g., deposits) but not when one wants to use them; thus justice is valuable in contexts of custody rather than active use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates shows this yields awkward conclusions (the just man would be a better thief/keeper than a user), and presses the interlocutors to consider whether this captures the moral import of justice; the point is explored via examples (keeping pruning-hooks, shields, lyres).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest blessing of wealth for the good: peace of mind (no need to deceive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cephalus' moral observation: for a good man, wealth's chief blessing is that it removes temptation/need to deceive or defraud, allowing a peaceful conscience in old age and freedom from fear about offerings/debts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is advanced as a justification for why Cephalus regards wealth positively in old age: not for pleasures but for moral peace; it frames an ethical criterion for assessing the value of wealth tied to moral conduct.
